Capitalism is an economic system based on the private ownership of the means of production and its use for the purpose of obtaining profit.

Designated Crown Prince during his father's 1967 coronation, this dissident has lived in exile in the US since the 1979 revolution that abolished the monarchy his family once ruled — who is he?
Reza Pahlavi: Former Crown Prince of Iran (born 1960)
Valedictorian of Plains High School in Georgia, this American first lady became a lifelong champion of mental health and women's rights — who was she?
Rosalynn Carter: First Lady of the United States from 1977 to 1981.
Nominated by President George W. Bush in 2005, this jurist became just the second Italian American justice on the Supreme Court, after Antonin Scalia — who is he?
Samuel Alito: US Supreme Court justice since 2006.
Named after a 1968 Czechoslovak uprising, this brief South Korean democratization movement began the night President Park Chung Hee was assassinated in 1979 — what is it called?
Seoul Spring: Period of democratization in South Korea (1979–1980)

Led by the future Roman emperor Titus, an army encircled and breached the walls of this Jewish holy city, destroying the Second Temple after a bitter feud between rival factions cut off the population's own food supply — which historic event is this?
Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE): Part of the First Jewish–Roman War.
Wounded at Gallipoli before entering politics, this businessman led the Nationalist Party as the eighth prime minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929 — who was he?
Stanley Bruce: Prime Minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929. In office, Bruce pursued an energetic and diverse agenda.
He led the first government of Bangladesh as prime minister during the 1971 War of Independence and is seen as one of the most instrumental figures in the nation's birth — who was he?
Tajuddin Ahmad: Prime Minister of Bangladesh from 1971 to 1972.
This crime-busting New York governor famously prosecuted mobster "Lucky" Luciano, then lost the presidency twice — to FDR in 1944 and Truman in 1948 — who was he?
As chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority, this Royal Court adviser also owned Spanish club Almería from 2019 to 2025 — who is he?
A free-love advocate and women's rights activist, she ran for president of the United States in 1872 — widely cited as the first woman to do so; who was she?
Victoria Woodhull: American women's suffrage activist (1838–1927)

Sparked by the 1791 Declaration of Pillnitz, this 1792–1797 conflict saw a loose alliance of European monarchies invade Revolutionary France, including the Duke of Brunswick's capture of Verdun — what was it called?
Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
War of the First Coalition: 1792–1797 wars between France and European powers.
Born to mixed English-American parentage, this statesman led his nation through its darkest hour as Prime Minister during World War II. Who?
Winston Churchill: British statesman and writer (1874–1965)
This Central European nation emerged after World War I as a union of South Slavic peoples, survived until 1992, and was born from the merger of Serbia with a provisional state. What country was this?
Which one below was born first?

Stephen Gray (scientist) (born 1666) is the earliest of the four. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Who among these was born first?
Emanuel Swedenborg (born 1688) is the earliest of the four.

Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four. Originally specified in the late 1950s, it is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in common use, after Fortran.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
SQL (founded 1974) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below is best known as an astronomer?
Edwin Hubble is an astronomer. Edwin Powell Hubble (November 20, 1889 – September 28, 1953) was an American astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Isaac Newton is a mathematician. Newton contributed to and refined the scientific method, and his work is considered the most influential in bringing forth modern science.
What is the atomic number of Caesium?
Caesium (IUPAC spelling; also spelled cesium in American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Cs and atomic number 55.
What is the atomic number of Tungsten?
Tungsten (also called wolfram) is a chemical element; it has symbol W (from German: Wolfram) and atomic number 74.
In what year was Saint Valentine born?
Saint Valentine was a clergyman – either a priest or a bishop – in the Roman Empire who ministered to persecuted Christians.
In what year was Doc Holliday born?
Doc Holliday: Holliday is best known for his role in the events surrounding and his participation in the gunfight at the O.K.
In what year was Johannes Kepler born?
Johannes Kepler (27 December 1571 – 15 November 1630) was a German polymath who was an astronomer, mathematician, astrologer, natural philosopher and music theorist.
In what year did William James Sidis die?
William James Sidis: Born to Boris Sidis, a prominent psychiatrist, and Sarah Mandelbaum Sidis, a physician, Sidis demonstrated extraordinary intellectual capabilities from infancy.
In what year did Thomas Edison die?
Thomas Edison: Thomas Alva Edison (February 11, 1847 – October 18, 1931) was an American inventor and businessman.
In what year was Helium discovered?
Helium: Helium (from Ancient Greek: ἥλιος, romanized: helios, lit. 'sun') is a chemical element; it has symbol He and atomic number 2.
Mil Mi-24: Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant. It is produced by Mil Moscow Helicopter Plant and was introduced by the Soviet Air Force in 1972.
Which country is General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon from?
General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon: United States. The aircraft was first developed by General Dynamics in 1974.
HTML: United Kingdom. Hypertext Markup Language (HTML) is the standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a web browser.
Who is credited with discovering Moscovium?
Moscovium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Moscovium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Mc and atomic number 115.
Who is credited with discovering Oxycodone?
Oxycodone: Martin Freund. It is a highly addictive and commonly abused drug.
Who is credited with discovering Germanium?
Germanium: Clemens Winkler. Germanium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ge and atomic number 32.
Heading Switzerland's Federal Department of Home Affairs for over a decade, this politician succeeded Marija Pejčinović Burić atop a major European institution in 2024 — who is he?
Alain Berset (French; born 9 April 1972) is a Swiss politician who served as a Member of the Swiss Federal Council from 2012 to 2023.
With a wingspan up to 3.3 meters and a weight of 15 kilograms, which South American bird is generally considered the largest bird of prey on Earth, sporting a ruff of white feathers around its neck?
Andean condor (Vultur gryphus) is a South American New World vulture and is the only extant member of the genus Vultur.
This red giant is the brightest star in the constellation Boötes and the fourth-brightest star in the entire night sky — name the star?
Arcturus is a red giant star in the northern constellation of Botes, and the brightest star in the constellation.
Born in 1655, this Italian instrument maker earned lasting fame for inventing a keyboard instrument that could play both soft and loud — who was he?
Bartolomeo Cristofori (Italian; May 4, 1655 - January 27, 1731) was an Italian maker of musical instruments famous for inventing the piano.
Despite its name, this sub-Saharan snake is actually grey to dark brown — the second-longest venomous snake in the world after the king cobra, commonly reaching 3 meters — name this species?
Black mamba (Dendroaspis polylepis) is a species of highly venomous snake belonging to the family Elapidae.
With a mass roughly 13 to 80 times Jupiter's, these substellar objects glow faintly from deuterium fusion rather than true hydrogen burning — what's the term for them?
Brown dwarf are substellar objects that have more mass than the biggest gas giant planets, but less than the least massive main-sequence stars.
Its name comes from the Latin for "coal," and one of its isotopes decays with a 5,700-year half-life that lets scientists date ancient remains — which element is it?
Carbon (from Latin carbo 'coal') is a chemical element; it has symbol C and atomic number 6.
Along with the bonobo, which great ape of equatorial Africa's forests and savannas is humans' closest living relative, according to DNA and fossil evidence?
Chimpanzee (Pan troglodytes), also simply known as the chimp, is a medium-sized great ape species found in the forests and savannas of equatorial Africa.
This digestive condition refers to swelling or inflammation of the large intestine, and can be acute and short-lived or a long-term, chronic issue — what is it called?
Colitis is swelling or inflammation of the large intestine (colon). It broadly fits into the category of digestive diseases.
These echinoderms come in stalked "sea lily" and free-swimming "feather star" forms, with mouths on their upper surface ringed by feeding arms — what class of marine animal is it?
Crinoid are marine invertebrates that make up the class Crinoidea.

Generally moving particles, energy, or other quantities from regions of higher concentration to lower, this stochastic physical process is driven by a gradient in Gibbs free energy and can occasionally even run 'uphill' via spinodal decomposition — name this process?
Diffusion is the net movement of anything (for example, atoms, ions, molecules, energy) generally from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
This American physicist was the first to make a transuranium element, neptunium, sharing the 1951 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Glenn Seaborg. Who was he?
Edwin McMillan (September 18, 1907 - September 7, 1991) was an American physicist credited with being the first to produce a transuranium element, neptunium.
This recurring set of hormone-driven reproductive changes in female mammals is interrupted by 'rest' phases and pregnancy, and has a male equivalent called rut — what is it?

Estrous cycle (from Latin oestrus 'frenzy', originally from Ancient Greek (ostros) 'gadfly') is a set of recurring physiological changes induced by reproductive hormones in females of mammalian subclass Theria.
Found on sperm cells, fungal spores and countless microbes, this tail-like structure provides motility and even senses moisture in some swarming bacteria — what is it?

Flagellum (pl.: flagella) (Latin for 'whip' or 'scourge') is a hair-like appendage that protrudes from certain plant and animal sperm cells, from fungal spores (zoospores), and from a wide range of microorganisms to provide motility.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can contain up to 6% caffeine — roughly double the concentration found in green coffee beans — and flavor a popular Brazilian soft drink. Name the plant?
Guarana (from the Portuguese guaran; Paullinia cupana, syns.

This colorless, nearly odorless organic compound is a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms, widely used as a cheap, largely unreactive solvent and found in small amounts in modern gasoline blends — what is it?
Hexane is an organic compound, a straight-chain alkane with six carbon atoms and the molecular formula C6H14.
Marked by shivering and confusion in mild cases and hallucinations or paradoxical undressing in severe cases, this condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35°C (95°F) — name it?
Hypothermia is defined as a body core temperature below 35.0 C (95.0 F) in humans.
A pioneer of radio microwave optics who also wrote science fiction and has a lunar crater named for him, this Indian polymath founded Asia's first interdisciplinary research institute — who was he?
Jagadish Chandra Bose (30 November 1858 - 23 November 1937) was an Indian polymath with interests in biology, physics and writing science fiction.
This occupation and set of methods involves producing and distributing reports on events and people that make up the 'news of the day,' with a commitment to accuracy — what is it?
Journalism is the production and distribution of reports on events, facts, ideas, and people that constitute the "news of the day" and inform society with a commitment to accuracy and verification.
Depicted as the goddess Minerva, this Italian physicist became the first woman with a science doctorate and the first salaried female university teacher. Who was she?
Laura Bassi (29 October 1711 - 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.
Prized as one of the most profitable seafood commodities in the coastal waters where it's caught, this clawed crustacean spends its life in crevices and burrows on the sea floor - which creature?
Lobster are malacostracan decapod crustaceans of the family Nephropidae or its synonym Homaridae.
Its bell-shaped flowers give way to yellow or orange berries, but this nightshade genus is better known by the folkloric root that inspired countless myths and superstitions — which genus?
Mandragora (genus) is a plant genus belonging to the nightshade family (Solanaceae).
Aristotle called this the 'first philosophy' — the branch that probes the most fundamental structure of reality, from existence itself to the categories of being — what is it?
Metaphysics is the branch of philosophy that examines the basic nature or most fundamental structure of reality.
Named for the river near which its type fossil was found by a Dutch chalk quarry in the 18th century, this genus of marine reptile lived until the end of the Cretaceous — what is it?
Mosasaurus ("lizard of the Meuse River") is the type genus (defining example) of the Mosasauridae, an extinct group of aquatic squamate reptiles.

An English aeronautical engineer who wrote novels like On the Beach and A Town Like Alice, he adopted a pen name specifically so his employers at Vickers wouldn't think him 'not a serious person.' Who is he?
Nevil Shute (17 January 1899 - 12 January 1960) was an English novelist and aeronautical engineer who spent his later years in Australia.
Which applied-math discipline, born from pre-WWII military planning and overlapping heavily with industrial engineering, hunts for the maximum profit or minimum cost in real-world problems?

Operations research (British), often shortened to the initialism OR, is a branch of applied mathematics that deals with the development and application of analytical methods to improve management and decision-making.
Native to the islands of Southeast Asia, this bushy perennial herb in the mint family is prized for a fragrant essential oil used widely in perfumery — what plant is it?
Patchouli (also spelled patchouly or pachouli; Pogostemon cablin) is a species of flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae, commonly called the mint or deadnettle family.
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive, and persistent fear of a specific object or situation, often leading sufferers to go to great lengths to avoid it — what is it called?
Phobia is an anxiety disorder, defined by an irrational, unrealistic, persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
Ranging from linear chains to heavily branched polymers, these carbohydrate compounds — like starch, glycogen, and chitin — consist of many simple sugar units linked together. What are they called?
Polysaccharide (from Ancient Greek (pols) 'many, much' and (skkhar) 'sugar') are "compounds consisting of a large number of monosaccharides linked glycosidically".

Harvested from the seeds of several Plantago species, this common dietary fiber supplement relieves both constipation and mild diarrhea, and occasionally doubles as a food thickener — what is it called?
Psyllium is the common name used for several members of the plant genus Plantago whose seeds are used commercially for the production of mucilage.

This genus of roughly 60 herbaceous perennials in the buckwheat family includes the familiar pie vegetable prized for its tart stalks despite mildly toxic leaves — which genus, native to Europe and Asia?
Rheum (plant) is a genus of about 60 herbaceous perennial plants in the family Polygonaceae.
This grayish-leaved, purple-flowered evergreen subshrub is a Mediterranean member of the mint family, long used both as a culinary herb and an ornamental garden plant — what plant is it?
Salvia officinalis is a perennial, evergreen subshrub, with woody stems, grayish leaves, and blue to purplish flowers.

This dog breed from southern China, traditionally kept as a property guardian, was driven to the brink of extinction in the 20th century and is known in the West for its deep wrinkles. What breed is this?

Shar Pei (Cantonese; pinyin: sh p) is a dog breed from
southern China.
This family of roughly 1,450 moth species, with narrow wings and streamlined bodies built for fast, hovering flight, are so nimble they're routinely mistaken for hummingbirds — what are they called?
Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms.
These large waterfowl of the genus Cygnus are close relatives of geese and ducks, and are known for typically mating for life. What birds are they?
Swan are birds of the genus Cygnus within the family Anatidae.
Classed among the saurischians and placing them nearer to sauropodomorphs than to ornithischians, these hollow-boned, three-toed dinosaurs were ancestrally meat-eaters — which clade?
Theropoda (from ancient Greek -) is one of the three major clades of dinosaur, alongside Ornithischia and Sauropodomorpha.

Native only to New Zealand and resembling a lizard, this reptile is the sole surviving member of an order that was hugely diverse in the Mesozoic era, with fossils dating to the Middle Triassic — what's the animal?
Tuatara (Mori:; Sphenodon punctatus) is a species of reptile endemic to New Zealand.

First described by John Edward Gray in 1821, this family of small feliform mammals spans Africa, southern Europe, and Asia on both sides of the Wallace Line, and includes the genets — name the family?
Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
Native from Panama to southern Canada, this plant genus of 50 species belongs to the asparagus family alongside the agaves — name the genus?
Yucca (YUK-) is both the scientific name and common name for a genus native to North America from Panama to southern Canada.
This protrusion in the neck, formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage around the larynx, becomes more prominent in most men during puberty — what is it?
Adam's apple: Feature of the neck. The Adam's apple is the protrusion in the neck formed by the angle of the thyroid cartilage surrounding the larynx, typically visible in men and less so in women.

This organic functional group, structured R−CH=O and alternatively called a formyl group when isolated from its side chain, appears throughout biologically and technologically important chemicals — what is it?
Aldehyde: Organic compound containing the functional group R–CH=O.

Once sold as Elavil, this tricyclic antidepressant is now often a second-line choice — used as much for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and migraines as for depression, thanks to its many side effects. Which drug?
Amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant. Due to the frequency and prominence of side effects, amitriptyline is generally considered a second-line therapy for these indications.
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois won the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering work on superfluidity and the quantum physics of low-temperature helium — who was he?
Painting, sculpture, and architecture are its three classical visual branches, yet nobody can agree on a single definition for it; what cultural pursuit of creative and imaginative talent is this?
Art: Creative work to evoke aesthetic response.
The world's largest nocturnal primate, this Madagascar lemur has ever-growing rodent-like teeth and taps tree trunks with a bony middle finger to fish out grubs by echo — which animal?
Aye-aye: Species of primate. This foraging method is called percussive foraging, and takes up 5–41% of the aye-aye's foraging time.
Named after the aromatic resin from which it was first derived, this simplest aromatic carboxylic compound forms salts widely used as food preservatives — what is it called?
This crested songbird in the crow family sports a black, U-shaped collar and is known for hiding acorns to eat later — which eastern North American bird?
Blue jay: Species of bird. The blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata) is a passerine bird in the family Corvidae, native to eastern North America.

Unique among mammals, human females are the only ones to permanently develop this secondary sex organ at puberty rather than just during pregnancy, and it later produces milk via the mammary gland — which body part?
Breast: Part of the female primate torso that has mammary glands.
The fifth most abundant element in Earth's crust and a reactive alkaline earth metal, this element's name comes from the Latin word for 'lime' obtained by heating limestone — what is it?
Calcium: Chemical element with atomic number 20 (Ca)
This compound ferries long-chain fatty acids into a cell's mitochondria to be burned for energy and is naturally concentrated in muscles like the heart — what is it?
Carnitine: Compound active in mitochondria. Carnitine is a quaternary ammonium compound involved in metabolism in most mammals, plants, and some bacteria.
In calculus, this formula computes the derivative of a composite function by multiplying together the derivatives of its two component functions — what is it called?

Native to Sri Lanka, the inner bark of this evergreen tree is the original source of a beloved baking spice, sometimes distinguished from a cheaper cousin as the 'true' or 'Ceylon' variety — which tree?
Cinnamomum verum: Species of tree. The inner bark of the tree is historically regarded as the spice cinnamon, though this term was later generalized to include C. cassia as well.
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Produced mainly by the adrenal cortex and surging in response to stress and low blood sugar, this steroid hormone is sold as medicine under the name hydrocortisone — what is it?
Built from microfilaments, intermediate filaments, and microtubules, this network gives a cell its shape and lets it contract and migrate — what is it?
Cytoskeleton: Network of filamentous proteins that forms the internal framework of cells.
Carnations and sweet williams both belong to which flowering plant genus of about 340 species, native mainly to Europe and Asia?
Attracted to rotting fruit and fermenting drinks, this insect became the first animal launched into space in 1946 and has earned six Nobel Prizes for scientists who studied it — what is it?
Drosophila melanogaster: Species of fruit fly.
The first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, this political scientist earned it in 2009 for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons — who was she?
This term covers a range of spiritual traditions built around hidden or occult knowledge, appearing in Christian, Buddhist, Hindu, and Quranic contexts alike — what is it?
Esotericism: Topics referred to by the same term.
What is this — “Public exposure of intimate body parts”?

Exhibitionism: Public exposure of intimate body parts. Exhibitionism is the practice of exposing one's intimate parts – such as the breasts, genitals, or buttocks – in a public or semi-public environment.

Sometimes nicknamed a 'cat' though it's actually the sole living member of its own genus in the weasel family, this North American forest mammal has been trapped for its fur since the 1700s — what is it?
Fisher (animal): Species of small, carnivorous mammal native to North America.

In math, this concept assigns exactly one element of a codomain to each element of a domain, and was formalized via set theory by the end of the 19th century after originating as a way to describe how one varying quantity depends on another — what is it called?
Function (mathematics): Association of one output to each input.
Recognized as the world's longest ray-finned fish, this ribbon-shaped, silvery-blue deep-sea creature is often blamed for sea-serpent legends — which fish?
Giant oarfish: Species of oceanic ray-finned fish.
Descended from medieval hunting dogs once used to take down bears, boar, and deer for German nobility, this breed ties with the Irish Wolfhound as one of the world's two largest — which breed is it?
Great Dane: German breed of dog. The Great Dane is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.
This German-American physicist won a 1967 Nobel Prize for explaining how a nuclear cycle powers heavy stars, after heading the Theoretical Division at Los Alamos during World War II — who is he?
In this condition, part of the stomach slips upward through the diaphragm into the chest, often triggering acid reflux, heartburn, or trouble swallowing — what is it?
Hiatal hernia: Entrance of abdominal organs into the middle chest through the diaphragm.
Also called prussic acid, this toxic, flammable liquid with the formula HCN boils just above room temperature and serves as an industrial precursor to plastics and mining chemicals — what is it?

Also known as the spectacled or binocellate snake, this reptile from South Asia is one of the 'Big Four' species responsible for most snakebites in the region and is revered in Hindu mythology — which snake?
Indian cobra: Species of snake. The species is native to the Indian subcontinent, and is a member of the "Big Four" species that are responsible for the most snakebite cases in Sri Lanka and India.
This English inventor and industrial designer created the bagless vacuum cleaner using cyclonic separation, and by 2023 was the UK's fifth-richest person — who is he?
James Dyson: British inventor and businessman (born 1947)
Back in 1859, this Irish physicist proved the link between atmospheric CO2 and what we now call the greenhouse effect — who was he?
Deafened by childhood illness and rerouted from competitive diving, she became a Hollywood stunt pioneer and earned the title 'the fastest woman in the world.' Who was she?
Kitty O'Neil: American stuntwoman and racer (1946–2018)
Spread through the bite of sandflies, this parasitic disease can appear in cutaneous, mucocutaneous, or visceral forms, the last marked by fever and an enlarged spleen — what is it called?
Leishmaniasis: Disease caused by parasites of the Leishmania type.

This catch-all name covers over 7,000 squamate species on every continent but Antarctica — from finger-length geckos to the three-meter Komodo dragon, with a few 'legless' lineages thrown in. What is it?
Found from Gibraltar to across Asia, these Old World monkeys live in troops centered on dominant matriarchs, and one Malaysian species eats about 70 rats a year — what are they?
Macaque: Genus of Old World monkeys. The macaques constitute a genus (Macaca) of gregarious Old World monkeys of the subfamily Cercopithecinae.
Prized by fur trappers for its yellowish-to-dark-brown coat, this bushy-tailed, weasel-like mammal is adapted to life in the taiga's coniferous forests — what is it?
Nicknamed 'Swallow' as a fighter and 'Storm Bird' as a bomber, this German aircraft was the world's first operational jet-powered fighter, first flying on jet power in 1942 — what was it?
Messerschmitt Me 262: First operational jet-powered fighter aircraft. The design of what would become the Me 262 started in April 1939, before World War II.

This Serbian polymath — mathematician, astronomer, civil engineer — explained Earth's long-term climate swings by tracking our planet's shifting position relative to the Sun, a theory of cycles that now bears his name. Who was he?
Milutin Milanković: Serbian scientist and professor (1879–1958)
This Bangladeshi economist founded Grameen Bank and pioneered modern microcredit, winning the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize before later leading an interim government — who is he?
Muhammad Yunus: Bangladeshi economist and statesman (born 1940)
Carried harmlessly in the noses of about 10% of adults, this bacterium is the only cause of bacterial meningitis known to occur in epidemics, especially across Africa and Asia — which microbe?
Neisseria meningitidis: Species of bacterium that can cause meningitis.
Designed in the late 1950s as a privately funded project, this small twin-engine fighter was built cheap to buy and maintain, making it a hugely popular export jet — what is it?
Northrop F-5: US lightweight low-cost fighter aircraft.
Named by analogy to how organs serve the body, what term describes a specialized, function-specific subunit within a biological cell?

Organelle: Specialized subunit within a cell. The name organelle comes from the idea that these structures are parts of cells, as organs are to the body, hence organelle, the suffix -elle being a diminutive.
Often triggered by nail-biting or frequent hand-washing, this inflammation of the skin around the nail is usually bacterial when sudden and fungal when it drags on — what is it called?
Paronychia: Inflammation of skin surrounding a nail. Its sudden (acute) occurrence is usually due to the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus.

Caused by a lack of intrinsic factor — often from an autoimmune attack on the stomach — this vitamin B12 deficiency disorder brings gradual fatigue, a smooth red tongue, and numbness in the hands and feet — which condition?
Pernicious anemia: Lack of red blood cells due to vitamin B12 deficiency.
Resembling a round, tailless rabbit with short ears, this small mountain-dwelling mammal's Himalayan relative lives at elevations above 6,000 meters — what animal is it?
Pika: Genus of mountain-dwelling mammal. A pika ( PY-kə, PEE-kə) is a small, mountain-dwelling mammal native to Asia and North America.
This succulent plant in the family Portulacaceae has every part edible, whether raw or cooked, and is also known by folk names like little hogweed — what is it, scientifically speaking?
Portulaca oleracea: Species of plant in the purslane family.

This noncontagious autoimmune disease shows up as dry, scaly red or purple patches, and injuring the skin can trigger new lesions right at that spot — a quirk called the Koebner phenomenon — what is it?
Psoriasis: Autoimmune diseases of the skin. Psoriasis is a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune disease characterized by patches of abnormal skin.

Born Richard Alpert, this spiritual teacher researched psychedelics with Timothy Leary at Harvard before writing the 1971 bestseller Be Here Now, popularizing Eastern spirituality in the West. What name did he later take?
As chairman of Purdue Pharma, this physician-businessman oversaw the launch of OxyContin and was later portrayed in the miniseries Dopesick and Painkiller — who is he?

Formed by the fusion of five vertebrae between the ages of 18 and 30, this triangular bone sits at the base of the spine and connects to the tailbone below and the last lumbar vertebra above. What is it?
Sacrum: Bone of the spine. The sacrum situates at the upper, back part of the pelvic cavity, between the two wings of the pelvis.
Covered in a spiny shell called a test and moving via tiny tube feet, this globular ocean-floor animal grazes mostly on algae — what creature is it?
Sea urchin: Class of marine invertebrates.
This small, wingless, primitive insect gets its common name from its grey sheen and darting, fish-like movements — and its scientific name hints at a diet of sugars and starches. What is it?
Silverfish: Small land insect in the order Zygentoma.
This healthcare discipline treats disorders of voice, fluency, and swallowing, practiced by clinicians licensed under boards overseen by groups like ASHA — which field of study?
Belonging to a fish family whose fossils date back to the Late Cretaceous, these long-lived, late-maturing fish share their order with paddlefish and once swam as far as North Africa — what are they?
Pig-shaped with a short, flexible snout, this odd-toed ungulate mammal lives in the jungles of South and Central America and Southeast Asia, alongside equine and rhino relatives — which animal?
Covered in sharp spikes along its leaf margins to ward off herbivores, this prickly flowering plant's fluffy seed head is known as 'down.' What is it?
Thistle: Common name of a group of flowering plants.
Also known as the windpipe, this cartilaginous tube linking the throat to the lungs is reinforced by horseshoe-shaped rings of cartilage — what is it?
Trachea: Cartilaginous tube. The trachea extends from the larynx and branches into the two primary bronchi.
Carrying the placeholder symbol Ubb, this hypothetical element 122 is expected to sit within the 'island of stability' — what is its systematic IUPAC name?
Unbibium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 122 (Ubb)
This Russian-Canadian programmer co-founded Bitcoin Magazine in 2011 before deploying a rival blockchain platform in 2015 alongside Gavin Wood and Charles Hoskinson — who is he?

Caused by the deletion of about 27 genes on chromosome 7, this genetic disorder is known for an unusually outgoing, empathetic personality alongside visual-spatial learning challenges — which condition?
Williams syndrome: Genetic disorder. Williams syndrome (WS), also Williams–Beuren syndrome (WBS), is a genetic disorder that affects many parts of the body.
